title: Miami’s Best Cuban Restaurants
summary: In Miami, Cuban food isn’t just popular — it’s part of the city’s DNA. Waves of Cuban immigrants, especially from the 1960s onward, have shaped the local culture, bringing more than just stories of resilience — they have built a food scene that has become a daily rhythm for…
whatHappening: Eater Miami is highlighting the best Cuban restaurants in a city where Cuban cuisine is woven into the everyday fabric of life. The dining guide reflects how Cuban food has become central to Miami's identity and local culture.
whoInvolved: Eater Miami, a prominent food and dining publication, is documenting Miami's Cuban restaurant scene. The restaurants themselves represent the legacy of Cuban immigrants who arrived in waves, particularly from the 1960s onward following the Cuban Revolution.
whyMatters: Cuban restaurants in Miami are not merely dining destinations—they represent the cultural and demographic transformation of the city over the past six decades. Understanding where to eat Cuban food in Miami is understanding the city's history and the ongoing influence of Cuban immigration on American urban life.
articleBody:
Miami's relationship with Cuban cuisine runs deeper than most American cities' connection to any single culinary tradition. According to Eater Miami, Cuban food isn't just popular in the city—it's part of Miami's DNA. This status reflects the waves of Cuban immigration that reshaped South Florida, especially beginning in the 1960s when Cubans fled communist rule under Fidel Castro following the Cuban Revolution.

The Cuban presence in South Florida actually predates the mid-20th century. Earlier waves of Cuban immigration, dating back to the 19th century, saw wealthy Cuban Americans establishing cigar factories in Tampa, Florida, while political exiles fled attempts to overthrow Spanish colonial rule. But it was the massive migration to Miami in the decades after the Cuban Revolution that fundamentally transformed the city's character and culinary landscape.

Neighborhoods like Little Havana emerged as cultural anchors, home to Cuban exiles and immigrants from across Central and South America. These communities didn't simply transplant Cuban food into Florida—they embedded it into the daily rhythms of Miami life, making Cuban restaurants as essential to the city as they were to Havana itself. The food became more than nostalgia; it became sustenance and identity.

Today, Miami's Cuban restaurant scene encompasses everything from casual cafés serving café con leche and pastelitos to more elaborate dining establishments preserving traditional island recipes. Each restaurant carries forward not just recipes but the stories of resilience and adaptation that define the Cuban-American experience. The best Cuban restaurants in Miami function as cultural repositories, keeping alive traditions while also evolving with new generations.

The guide underscores why food journalism focused on Miami's dining scene inevitably centers on Cuban cuisine—it's impossible to tell Miami's story without acknowledging the Cuban immigration that built the modern city. For residents and visitors alike, exploring Miami's Cuban restaurants is exploring the city's foundation.

Local business owners and entrepreneurs have recognized the opportunity this presents. articleBody:
Miami Spice has long held a special place in the local dining calendar, offering residents and visitors alike a chance to experience the city's most acclaimed restaurants at accessible price points. But this year's iteration feels fundamentally different in scope and ambition. According to Digest Miami, restaurants are leaning into the season with exclusive dishes, premium ingredients, and thoughtful beverage pairings that signal a shift away from stripped-down prix-fixe basics toward genuine culinary creativity.

The shift reflects a maturing event. What began as a simple value proposition—eat at top restaurants for less—has evolved into something more complex. Restaurants are now using Miami Spice as an opportunity to test new menu concepts, collaborate with wine and spirits programs, and differentiate themselves through limited-time offerings. These exclusive dishes won't appear on regular menus, giving diners an incentive to participate during the designated season rather than simply booking a table any other time of year.

The emphasis on premium ingredients underscores a confidence among Miami's culinary community that diners are willing to engage with higher-end offerings during Miami Spice. Rather than view the event as an opportunity to clear inventory or cut costs, participating chefs are treating it as a showcase. This approach mirrors successful promotional seasons in other major cities, where high-end restaurants have discovered that limited-time menus at special prices can actually enhance rather than diminish their brand perception.

Beverage pairings have also become central to the 2026 strategy. title: Miami Spice Back with New Reserve Tier and 300 Restaurants
summary: The 25th edition of Miami Spice Restaurant Months is back from August 1 through September 30, 2026. This year’s program from The Greater Miami Convention & Visitors Bureau (GMCVB) features three-course prix-fixe menus at a minimum of 30% savings at more than 300 participating…

whoInvolved: The Greater Miami Convention & Visitors Bureau (GMCVB) is organizing the initiative, the official tourism promotion agency for the Miami area. The program brings together hundreds of independent and chain restaurants across the region to offer discounted dining experiences.

articleBody:
The Greater Miami Convention & Visitors Bureau is launching the 25th annual Miami Spice Restaurant Month, marking a quarter-century of the popular dining program. Running from August 1 through September 30, 2026, the initiative aims to invigorate Miami's food scene during the summer season while offering diners unprecedented value across the region's restaurant landscape.

This year's edition introduces a new reserve tier to the program's structure, expanding beyond the traditional format and giving participating establishments more flexibility in how they price and structure their offerings. The core program remains unchanged: more than 300 restaurants are participating, each offering three-course prix-fixe menus at a minimum of 30% savings compared to regular menu pricing. According to Miami Curated, the expanded framework reflects growing demand for diverse dining experiences at various price points.

Miami Spice has become a signature event in the region's culinary calendar, particularly important during summer months when tourism typically dips due to heat and hurricane season. The program has traditionally served dual purposes: attracting visitors during the slower season and giving locals affordable access to restaurants they might not otherwise frequent. With over 300 establishments now participating—a significant number given Miami's competitive restaurant market—the program demonstrates sustained support from both independent operators and larger dining groups.

The reserve tier addition suggests an evolution in how the GMCVB is approaching the program's core mission. By creating tiered options, the bureau may be accommodating both high-end establishments seeking to maintain brand positioning while still participating, and more casual venues targeting volume. This flexibility could attract restaurants previously hesitant to join due to concerns about margin erosion or brand dilution.

For Miami's hospitality sector, Miami Spice remains a critical tool for maintaining revenue momentum during historically challenging months. The program's longevity—now spanning 25 years—underscores its effectiveness as both a marketing tool and genuine value proposition. By concentrating promotional efforts into a defined two-month window, participating restaurants can maximize marketing efficiency while building anticipation among diners.

articleBody:
A new feature from Miami Curated celebrates five bars in Miami that exemplify elegance and refined hospitality, drawing parallels to iconic establishments that have long defined upscale cocktail culture in major American cities. The publication opens by referencing the King Cole Bar at the St. Regis in New York, a storied venue that evokes a sense of immersion into a bygone era when elegance was understood as a deeply desired way of life. The St. Regis New York itself, located at 2 East 55th Street at the corner of Fifth Avenue in Midtown Manhattan, stands as a testament to this aesthetic—originally developed by John Jacob Astor IV and completed in 1904 to designs by Trowbridge & Livingston, it has been operated by Marriott International and holds both Forbes five-star and AAA five-diamond ratings.

According to Miami Curated, the five Miami bars profiled in the feature share a commitment to preserving this sense of timeless sophistication at a moment when modern fashion and broader cultural trends have increasingly embraced casualness. The piece explores how these venues maintain their character and allure despite shifting consumer preferences, offering patrons an experience that deliberately stands apart from the ephemeral nature of trend-driven establishments.

The contrast between casual contemporary culture and the enduring appeal of elegant cocktail bars reflects a deeper dynamic in hospitality. While streetwear and relaxed aesthetics dominate mainstream fashion, venues that intentionally curate an atmosphere of refinement continue to attract those seeking respite from the everyday. The bars highlighted in Miami Curated's feature appear designed with this principle in mind—creating spaces where elegance remains not merely nostalgic but actively practiced.

Miami's bar scene has long competed for attention and patronage, with new venues constantly emerging. Features like this one, which elevate bars that prioritize atmosphere and classical design over novelty, may help distinguish establishments that offer lasting value over temporary appeal. By drawing connections to legendary spaces like the King Cole Bar, the publication frames these Miami venues within a broader tradition of sophisticated hospitality.

The feature ultimately suggests that for a meaningful segment of diners and drinkers, elegance retains its power as a draw—even, or perhaps especially, when it stands in deliberate contrast to prevailing cultural norms.
